Holds a partial wake lock for long tasks (CPU stays awake). Not guaranteed to beat this ROM’s freeze-on-screen-off behavior; a last-resort safeguard, at a small battery cost.
Whitelisted: less likely to be frozen (this ROM is aggressive; not a 100% guarantee)

No storage permission; files are read via SAF

A hash squeezes a file of any size into a fixed-length “fingerprint”. The same file always yields the same value; change one byte and the fingerprint changes completely; and the fingerprint can’t be turned back into the file.
After downloading, copying or backing up, compare against the fingerprint published by the source to confirm the file wasn’t corrupted or tampered with.
Tell if two things are identical
Two devices can compare fingerprints to know they hold the same content — without transferring the file.
Record a fingerprint at some moment; later you can prove the file hasn’t changed since.
Treat the fingerprint as the file’s ID card — duplicates are spotted at a glance.
They are all public standards; their security comes from being one-way and collision-resistant, not from secrecy.
Old and fast; but deliberate collisions have been demonstrated — kept only for compatibility with legacy checksums
Also broken in practice (SHAttered, 2017) — don’t use it for new work
The most common, safest choice today
Different grades of the SHA-2 family; SHA-512 uses 64-bit words internally, so its structure differs
The newer standard (Keccak); this app bundles an ARMv8.2 assembly implementation, ≈0.7–1.0 GB/s (≈0.3 GB/s when falling back to software)
Chinese national standard with strength similar to SHA-256; software-only in this app (no instruction path)
An error-detection checksum (common in .sfv lists); not a cryptographic hash — it can be forged
A “collision” means two different files producing the same fingerprint. Being able to construct collisions doesn’t mean the file can be reversed — but for anti-tampering purposes it is fatal enough.

Modern ARM CPUs carry dedicated hashing instructions. This app checks two things — whether the CPU has the instruction, and whether the implementation actually uses it (measured) — and only then lights the CPU badge.
Measured on this device (memory benchmark, disk excluded):
bundled assembly (EOR3); ≈0.3 GB/s if it falls back to software

In practice: a 1 GB file takes roughly 0.4–0.7 s with SHA-256. A software-only implementation is about an order of magnitude slower, which would make large-file and batch verification impractical. The instruction path also draws less power and runs cooler.

What isn’t accelerated: SM3 runs in pure software; SHA-3 has no system library, so the app carries its own ARMv8.2 assembly and falls back to software when unavailable — slower rather than wrong. CRC32 uses the platform’s native implementation and is very fast; it is a checksum, not a cryptographic hash.
A “long task” (≥64 MB) shows a persistent notification (a foreground service): harder to kill, harder to throttle, one-tap cancel. Small files won’t bother you.

Auto screen-off is blocked while computing by default. If you lock the screen manually, this ROM may still freeze the computation (in our tests, neither the foreground service nor the wake lock was exempt) — the switches in Settings and the battery whitelist are mitigations, not a cure.
The “done” alert only fires when the app is not in the foreground; cancelling yourself is not a failure and won’t notify.
SHA-256 and SHA-1 on by default
SHA-256 is the common default; SHA-1 is still used by many older lists, so it is computed alongside. Everything else is opt-in.
For one reason only: some old sites and documents publish only those values — to compare, you must be able to compute them.
Uppercase or lowercase hex is just a writing convention; the two spellings of a byte are treated the same when comparing.
A single file’s hash chain can’t be parallelized; hashing several files at once (1–8) is what lifts total throughput.
Speed numbers are measured on this device and vary with model and frequency tier; the conclusion “hardware ≫ software” holds regardless.
Persistent progress notification while computing (silent, not dismissible)
